title: God Breaks the Weapons of War
overview: This psalm celebrates God for crushing an army that threatened Jerusalem, and calls on people and nations to honor him.

parts.label: God at home in Jerusalem (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Salem is an old short name for Jerusalem, and Zion is the hill where the temple stood, pictured here as God's tent. The poet says it was there, at God's own city, that an enemy's arrows, shields and swords were smashed.

parts.label: Warriors who never wake (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: The enemy soldiers are not just beaten but dead, their sleep a picture of death, and even their horses and chariots lie still at one word of rebuke from God. The phrase about mountains 'rich with game' or 'of prey' is unclear, and may picture invaders as predators on the hills, with God shining far above them.

parts.label: God rises to judge (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The battle is described as a verdict spoken from heaven, and the whole land falls silent like a courtroom when the judge stands. The stated purpose is to rescue the 'afflicted' or 'meek', the powerless people of the land.

parts.label: Even human rage serves God (v. 10)
parts.note: This verse is hard to translate, and scholars are unsure of its exact sense. The main idea seems to be that human fury ends up bringing God praise, and whatever anger remains is held in check.

parts.label: Keep your promises (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: People who made vows, solemn promises to God often paired with an offering, are told to follow through, and neighboring nations are invited to bring gifts. The closing lines warn that God can break the pride of rulers and kings.

think: The psalm pictures a power that crushes armies yet acts to rescue the powerless. What, if anything, would make you trust a power that strong?
